01 / Operational theory

The fighter’s decision architecture

Replace automatic movement with a four-stage decision cycle. Learn to recognize the information your opponent gives you before spending dash or Saitama abilities.

The fundamental loop

Do not skip confirmation. Visual bait is not proof that an opponent has no defensive answer.

Your range rules

RangeDefault questionPrimary plan
FarWhere will they turn?Hook entry or feint; no blind rush
MidWhich escape will they spend?Hook / longarm mix or hold response
CloseIs there a confirmed opening?Longarm-style catch, M1 conversion, reset

Range labels are relative, not measured stud thresholds. Distance changes with movement, target facing, ping, and moves.

Information

What can they still do?

Watch side-dash, front/back dash, guard orientation, counter availability, M1 recovery, and which escape lanes they still have.

Commitment

What does your threat force?

One believable hook may provoke a panic side-dash. A false forward step may make a passive defender retreat. That reaction is your actual resource.

Conversion

What is confirmed?

Do not launch a long Saitama sequence just because you planned it. Select your route according to target stun, knockback, cooldown and recovery.

A / hook

Cross the line

Change lane before using a committed dash. The hit is at the opponent’s eventual position, not their frozen silhouette.

B / longarm

Catch the endpoint

Treat it as spacing and timing, not a measured hitbox extension.

C / orbit

Make them rotate

Use shallow elliptical approaches with brief switches; orbiting alone does not win neutral.

D / flick

Alter orientation

Record endpoint, recovery and contact before assuming a flick creates a novel dash state.

03 / Intent before input

Neutral, conditioning, tempo

Good 1v1s often hinge on what the other player expects you to do next. Build reversible plans, not autopilot patterns.

Four-step approach rhythm

The strongest feint is credible. If your first entry never threatened a hit, the defender has no reason to bite on the second one.

Read hierarchy

ObserveMeaningResponse
Early side dashThey react to your entry cueFeign then endpoint punish
Constant backward driftPreserve open spaceIntercept diagonal escape
Hold block on M1 rangeWaiting for free punishAngle / guardbreak / reset
Fast turn to your hook sideThey learned your patternSwitch lane or delay
Dash immediately on get-upPredictable wake escapeCover likely endpoint
Moves only after you missReactive punish styleFake commit, stop outside punish

When ahead on HP

Do not turn aggression into random commitments. Force your opponent to open, deny high-value routes, keep dash resources and fight at safe angles.

When equal on HP

Measure the first two reactions, then deliberately change one variable: approach side, rhythm, or distance. Keep the other variables stable.

When behind on HP

Take purposeful risks that have a route to damage. Panic chasing into a defender’s M1 is not aggression; passivity without creating reads is not safety.

The green / yellow / orange / red model

Green

Dominant HP → controlled pressure

Yellow

Near parity → test & condition

Orange

Unfavorable → higher-quality commitments

Red

Critical → survive and exploit actual openings

Colors represent a voluntary decision framework, not official in-game states or rigid numerical laws. HP lead, matchup and cooldown matter more than a single percentage.

    Performance / common misreads

    Three techniques, three different problems

    Endlag bait

    Opponents who counterdash

    They believe your attack or recovery leaves you open. The trap is not the fake itself; it is the block/punish setup that makes their response expensive.

    Counterplay: they stop dashing on cue, delay, change the angle, or use a guard bypass.

    M1 catch

    Opponents who dash from far

    You place the M1 to intercept their approaching lane. Better angle and distance can matter more than trying to hit a perfect millisecond.

    Counterplay: they stop short, curve outside the hit lane, or make you swing early.

    Khai dash

    Overcommitted dash users

    Reactive counter-entry against predictable approach shapes, including repeated hookdash and longarm. Only use the spacing where you can see and intercept.

    Counterplay: delayed startups, fake entries, range changes, and late lane switches.

    Terminology: “Preblock” and “ghost block” are retained from your notes. Your notes call out both in the Endlag Bait footage; they do not specify a unique key sequence or verify undocumented engine behavior. Both have dedicated entries in the technique library to test them properly.

    How to strafe

    You should strafe mainly like in the video.

    • DO NOT get SO close to your opponent, otherwise you will mess up.
    • Only use it if you have no dashes left, or if you want to space away to punish your opponent.
    • DO NOT overstrafe. You get punished easily, and it can end in a combo or even a death combo.

    Player notes / Star + community

    Spacing, HP & habit notes

    Short rules of thumb collected from Star and other players. Tips carry the name of whoever said them.

    Player-reported
    Star spacing

    Oval walk

    If you’re going passive, walk an oval (half oval) around them while looking at them, at about a 45° angle.

    HP & TEMPO

    When to be aggro

    Green HP / 60%+Aggro
    Both neon yellowAggro, not too
    Below 60%Passive
    Survival

    Low HP & the ground

    • At 25% HP or less, just run.
    • When you’re on the ground, try not using RC and time the backdash right.
    Khai dash

    Answer to the longarm

    • If they do a longarm, try a Khai dash.
    • A Khai dash is like a “J” around them (or around the longarm). It’s a high-to-middle HP move.
    • Do an M1 first, so that when the 2nd M1 hits you catch them cleanly (Khai and hook move).
    • Sometimes you need a tiny MINI PAUSE.
    HOOK & LONGARM

    Pick by range

    • Far: don’t longarm at range — use hooks. A far longarm is predictable and easy to react to.
    • Near / they come close: try the longarm.
    • KerYou can always do one random longarm, every few rounds.
    • Don’t longarm instantly after a hook backdash. You’re close and can get punished because of the cooldown.
    • 4nti / Raxind2 M1 → sidedash → M1 → sidedash → M1 is basically a normal longarm.
    M1 habits

    Catch, delay, trade

    • Stop spamming Consecutive Punches — use Shove instead.
    • Always try to M1 catch with a C dash (or similar) after the 1st–2nd M1.
    • Do your M1 a bit later to delay them, and block earlier, for better M1 trades and faster M1ing.
    • StarM1 → dash → M1 to get someone.
    • PepsiWhen someone holds block and you have Shove, always use Shove.
    Shove dash

    High commitment

    • Only use it on mid / high HP. Otherwise it’s a free counterdash for the opponent.
    • Don’t use it on high FPS.
    • If the opponent abuses Shove Dash, just counterdash it. It’s a high-commitment move, so it’s a free counter.
    Dash range

    Your dash shrinks as HP drops

    Your HPFront dashSide dash
    Max HP4 tiles3 tiles
    Orange HP3.5 tiles2.6 tiles
    Red HP (very low)3 tiles2 tiles

    Be extra careful when the opponent is at max HP — their dash reaches furthest.

    Movement tricks

    Credited tips from players

    • Elm / JiroTurn on directional dash so you don’t need to hold Shift constantly. The dash goes where your screen is facing, for every dash except the front dash.
    • ElmNormally just front dash (FD) or side dash on a slight angle to the person, then FD.
    • PashaRare, but: walk toward the opponent after a 4 move, then jump and M1 to catch them in the air, to vary your play.
    • WilsFront dash, but flick when you hit the opponent’s back. Because TSB hitboxes are bad, you land at their back. Aim slightly to the side and flick; it’s a straight front dash.
    • Sbz / 1h str starMake a 360° spin after a hook backdash.
    • PepsiTry jumping on someone’s head maybe once a round. If they can see it easily, don’t do it.
    • TarietityTo troll: walk away, then come back at them with a C dash back (shaped like a “C”). Rare people do that.
    • Jump before dash and walk with the jump to gain range: about 3 tiles becomes 3.75 tiles.

    Numbers and timings are player-reported and can shift with patches, FPS and ping. Check them in a practice session before relying on them.

    06 / Interactive network science

    Ping, hitboxes, and perceived range

    Experiment with both players’ latency and jitter. Learn what a displayed ping does measure, what it does not, and how it changes decision quality.

    Do not make the common mistake: 100 ms ping does not mean “a 100 ms bigger hitbox” or a fixed extra attack reach. TSB’s exact server collision, compensation, timing windows and network implementation are not publicly established here. The visual model below is a deliberately simplified teaching tool.

    The drawn rings are fictional actor markers; true colliders, animation timing, server-side tests and any lag compensation are unknown. This graphic only illustrates stale rendered positions.

    10 ms increments: practical field guidance

    Simplified calculations assume illustrative constant walking speed of 16 studs/s. The “neutral priority” column is coaching advice, not official server behavior. Your real TSB server, map and opponent movement may differ.

    When YOU have high ping

    Read farther ahead. Stand where the opponent will have to end, not where an older animation says they are. Confirm safer M1 openings before spending major moves.

    When OPPONENT has high ping

    Assume more uncertainty in what they see and how their inputs reach the server. Vary approach angle and avoid an untested universal “anti-lag” timing offset.

    When both ping and jitter rise

    Prefer stable movement, larger safety margins, and repeated paired tests. If position jumps between frames, focus on information reliability before blaming a hitbox.

    Controlled test protocol

    1. Use a consenting sparring partner in a private session.
    2. Record BOTH player ping readings and your FPS.
    3. Fix your start position and both players’ directions.
    4. Repeat the exact dash/M1 interaction 10+ times per bracket.
    1. Separate a visible animation contact from actual damage/stun.
    2. Change one factor: ping, movement, or jitter, never all at once.
    3. Record successful hits, whiffs, and suspicious snapshots.
    4. Retest after patches; the guide never asserts hidden hitbox sizes.

    Your prior TSB baseline was around 38–40 ms on favorable European servers. Use that as one reference condition, not a guarantee of every match’s actual latency.

    V3 field expansion • perception → range → reaction → adaptation

    Learn to see the hitbox

    Not a cheat overlay. Build an internal map of effective contact space from visible facing, approach lanes, repeated contact outcomes, and real ping conditions. The browser diagrams are teaching models, never extracted TSB collision data.

    Hitbox training
    Adapting fast, one step at a time

    Watch where the attack is going, not the body.

    Nu poți vedea direct hitbox-ul real în TSB din Chrome. What strong players learn to “see” is the effective hit region: which approach angle, range, facing, motion state and recovery lets an attack actually register. Treat each landed M1, clean whiff and block as a new measurement. Do not move your M1 timing randomly before checking your lane and distance.

    AnchorRead their core

    Track the avatar’s torso / feet center and travel direction; ignore large weapon VFX and flailing limbs as exact boundaries.

    CorridorRead facing + lane

    Estimate where the attack will pass, not only where the enemy was one moment ago. Observe turn, diagonal and escape path.

    ContactRead server outcome

    Damage, stun, knockback or blocked response counts as evidence; animation overlap alone is ambiguous.

    UpdateCorrect just one variable

    Change spacing first, then angle/facing, then response timing. Test the same cue again to avoid random guesses.

    Core ruleReact to the dash, not to a fixed timer. Only selectively pre-time when their repeated pattern makes the dash onset predictable. Your own ping does not reveal the opponent’s current server-authoritative position.
    Try it in a real match, no exploits

    How beginners start to “see” the contact area in 10 minutes

    Before the set

    1. Turn on Roblox performance information if available in the game settings; Roblox also documents Shift + F3 for the network stats overlay. Record ping + FPS as context, not an exact hitbox formula.
    2. Pick Saitama with one opponent and one attack. Stand on a repeatable floor reference.

    During the set

    3. Have them dash straight at you five times from a similar distance. Keep the opponent core in view. Identify the exact moment their lane becomes clear.
    4. Repeat from a closer start. Record hit/miss only when the game actually confirms it.

    After the set

    5. Watch the recording at reduced playback speed. Compare the facing angle, target center, and direction just before contact. Mark your reliable zone of success.
    6. Repeat with a curve or different ping; update your mental zone instead of memorizing a made-up collider size.

    Do not rely on Roblox Studio collision overlays in someone else's published experience: those debugging visualizations are not the same thing as public-game Saitama attack hitboxes.

    Interactive 04 · when it feels wrong

    Hitbox problem diagnostician

    Choose what you actually observed. The result prioritizes one experiment so you can adjust after just a few exchanges instead of replacing your whole fighting style.

    Pick a situation to get a two-exchange test plan.
    My M1 looks on target but does not damage. Why?

    Animation and visual effects are not necessarily collision checks. First verify your facing and the opponent’s motion state; then test a closer start with identical timing. A clean contact indicator matters more than a screenshot of apparent overlap.

    Why does a 100ms opponent seem to reach farther?

    The local view is a reconstructed, time-delayed presentation. With rapid movement and replication you might see an outdated or interpolated pose. The amount and direction cannot be inferred from ping alone, and TSB’s specific contact checks are not established by a simple RTT formula.

    Can I turn on hitbox outlines in a public TSB match?

    There is no confirmed built-in public TSB command to show its actual attack colliders. Roblox Studio debug visualizations belong to experiences you develop/test with permission; Chrome cannot inspect the live game's authoritative collision rules. Use repeated controlled contact tests instead of exploit scripts.

    Does FPS affect the hitbox?

    Low or unstable FPS affects how often you see new frames and potentially when you can respond. It does not prove that the game's server collision geometry changed. Measure ping, jitter and FPS separately.

    The 5-exchange routine

    Adapt faster than their next mix-up

    1. Exchange 1 — Scout.

      Do not force damage. Identify their favorite entrance (straight / hook / longarm), turning direction, and reaction to one fake recovery.

    2. Exchange 2 — Mark the boundary.

      Hold a stable camera. Let them approach from the same distance. Observe where a clean M1/block actually registers. Don't chase the visual limb.

    3. Exchange 3 — Adjust ONE axis.

      Change your lateral placement or move half a step nearer. Keep your response cue identical. If success changes, the issue was likely geometry, not a magical timing fix.

    4. Exchange 4 — Test a reactive counter.

      Randomize their dash start. React to commitment; M1 catch for a long lane, guard for counterdash bait, Khai dash for a readable intercept. Abort if they fake.

    5. Exchange 5 — Lock a conditional rule.

      “When X at Y spacing, I do Z; if they stop-short, I reset.” Retest whenever ping/jitter, opponent or move changes.

    Under pressure: Identify One cue, choose One response, observe One result. Do not change dash type, camera, distance and click timing at once.
    Decision geometry

    The M1 / guard / Khai priority chart

    If their dash is baited by apparent endlag, replace the initial offense with oriented preblock and punish recovery. If they stop-short, the correct answer may be no attack.

    Camera firstKeep the opponent and arrival corridor in frame. A correct read you cannot see is not a usable reaction.

    3-minute warm-up: eye training

    For 60 seconds, watch only the opponent's center, travel vector and feet; do not attack. For 60 seconds, call “front / left / right / stop” on every committed dash. For 60 seconds, M1-catch only confirmed long approaches. Score correct lane reads, not win rate.

    6-minute spacing calibration

    Record 5 attempts each at close, mid and edge range in one lane, with the same move. Move just one variable between batches. Compare hit rates, not individual weird frames. Mark what breaks when the opponent curves or stop-shorts.

    1-minute match reset

    Before your next set: ping bucket, FPS stability, dominant approach lane, opponent counterdash trigger and your last two whiffs. Choose the simplest correction. Your baseline near 38–40ms is a reference, not a promise that every EU game behaves the same.

    Hitbox + ping field notes

    Hitbox & ping playbook

    What ping really changes, how to adjust each technique to it, and a checklist for when a hit feels wrong.

    Coaching model · test it
    The basics

    What ping does, and doesn’t

    • You see your opponent where they were a moment ago. They see you the same way. The server decides what actually hit.
    • Ping doesn’t make a hitbox bigger. It changes how old your picture is and when your inputs arrive.
    • A hit that looks like a clean whiff, or the reverse, is usually that delay, not a different hitbox.
    • Jitter (ping that jumps around) is harder to play against than steady high ping.
    Your ping is high

    Give yourself margin

    • Block earlier and space farther away. Don’t wait for the last moment.
    • Don’t depend on reaction M1 catches or Khai dashes at the very edge of range.
    • Stand where they have to commit first, so you aren’t reacting to an old picture.
    • Skip long, committed moves like Shove Dash unless the opening is clearly confirmed.
    Their ping is high

    Use their older picture

    • Their view of you is older, so a flick or fake gets a late response. Bait it, then punish the dash.
    • Their dashes and blocks can arrive late or look like jumps. Don’t judge a read from one frame.
    • Vary your angle with a strafe or hook instead of walking straight in.
    • Keep your guard up. A lagging player can suddenly catch up.
    By technique

    Adjusting each technique to ping

    TechniqueWhen YOUR ping is highWhen THEIR ping is high
    M1 catchPlace the M1 on their dash lane earlier and from a bit farther back. Don’t react at the last moment.Their dash may show up late. Let it arrive, then catch where they end up.
    Khai dashStay farther from the edge of their longarm. A late picture makes the “J” path riskier.Their longarm may be late or jumpy. A mini pause before the second M1 helps.
    Flick baitKeep the flick small and close. Check that they reacted before you spend your dash.Their reaction comes late, so wait for it before you dash and punish.
    StrafeStay out of reach and keep moving. Overstrafing gets punished faster.Wide, changing strafes make their picture of you stale.
    CounterdashCounter as soon as you see them commit. Don’t wait to be sure.Don’t pre-time it. Wait for the dash to commit first.
    M1 trading / ghost blockBlock earlier. Trades can resolve later than they look.Keep blocking until the exchange clearly ends.

    This table is coaching advice built from the ping model above, not verified TSB behavior. Try each change in a private spar and keep what works for you.

    Range markers

    Measure with the floor

    • Floor tiles are your ruler. Learn how many tiles away you are before you commit.
    • Player-reported dash reach: 4 tiles front, 3 tiles side at max HP, down to 3 front, 2 side at very low HP. An opponent at max HP reaches farthest.
    • A jump before a dash can add about 0.75 tile (3 → 3.75), so leave a little extra room.
    • Ping adds uncertainty on top of these numbers. Stay slightly outside them when you can’t afford to be hit.
    When it feels wrong

    Check these before blaming the hitbox

    1. Ping and FPS. Check both. Very high FPS can also change dash timing, which is why players advise against Shove Dash on high FPS.
    2. Facing and lane. Were you actually pointed at where they ended up?
    3. Distance. Repeat the same exchange from slightly closer. Edge-of-range misses are normal.
    4. Their state. Were they dashing, stunned or blocking when it landed?
    5. Replay. Watch your recording at reduced speed and compare facing and distance just before contact.
    6. Change one thing. Adjust spacing, angle or timing, then repeat.
    Evidence discipline: A diagram in this guide cannot reveal a game's private attack geometry or server rewinds. “I got hit from behind” is an observation; “their hitbox increased by 2 studs because of 90ms ping” is not established by it. Validate in a live match with a consenting partner and compare both perspectives when possible.
    07 / Deny, evade, counter

    Defense & arena control

    A solid defender must understand facing, the opponent’s next destination, knockback lines and recovery—not only hold block.

    Facing / block angle model

    Conceptual front versus side pressure. Actual blockability depends on attack properties, game state, camera and current build.

    Ping & block timing

    Your ping is highBlock earlier, space farther
    Their ping is highExpect late dashes; punish the end position
    Ping keeps jumpingHold your guard; don’t trust one frame
    Low FPSInputs land later; play safer

    Coaching guidance, not verified TSB behavior. See the hitbox & ping playbook for details.

    Against auto-block

    Use a threat that rotates their facing, evaluate a verified guardbreak, or exit to reset. Do not finish a predictable M1 into their defended front.

    Against dash aggression

    Choose an escape lane before they start. Side movement that creates a whiff may be stronger than using your own front dash on reaction.

    Against a high-ping opponent

    Their picture of you is older. Vary your approach angle, bait their reaction, and punish where they end up rather than where they appear.

    Rules / match conduct

    Strike system

    What strikes are, how they stack, and what earns one.

    Q

    What are strikes?

    Strikes are given for excessive passiveness, lack of dashing, abusing banned techs, or looping the system.

    Q

    How does the strike system work?

    StrikesResult
    1 / 3No punishment
    2 / 3No punishment
    3 / 3Auto win
    Q

    What gives an automatic strike?

    • 2RC → auto point + strike
    • Floor glitch → auto point + strike

    A video will be provided showing what counts as a floor glitch.

    Q

    What counts as a passive strike?

    • Not dashing while being passive
    • Waiting for the opponent to dash instead of initiating
    • Running and dashing every 6–10 seconds
    • Only using counter dashes for a period of time
    • Corner camping or corner pushing
    • Dashing away from your opponent (does not count as a dash)
    Rules / play legal, play safe

    How to avoid a passive strike

    Strikes 1 and 2 carry no punishment, but the third is an auto win, so don’t treat them as free. Each passive strike has a legal way to play the same situation.

    Passive strikes

    What the rules punish, and what to do instead

    What earns the strikeDo this instead
    Not dashing while being passiveDash with a purpose. The hookdash is a C-type dash you can use any time, and it isn’t an aggro dash because you can’t easily be punished for it.
    Waiting for the opponent to dash instead of initiatingTake the first action: a hookdash entry, a flick bait or an M1 approach. Patient is fine. Waiting for them every time is not.
    Running and dashing every 6–10 secondsDon’t dash on a timer. Dash to bait, to space or to punish, and change the rhythm.
    Only using counter dashes for a period of timeCounterdash when they commit, then start something yourself, like a hookdash or an M1 catch.
    Corner camping or corner pushingKeep the fight in open space. Step out of corners and don’t herd them into one.
    Dashing away from your opponent (this does not count as a dash)A dash away doesn’t help you. Dash toward them, around them (hookdash) or to line up a punish.
    Automatic strikes

    No warning for these

    • 2RC (2 Ragdoll Cancel) gives an auto point and a strike. It’s illegal because it’s random, comes down to luck, and is a bug. Never chain a second RC.
    • Floor glitch gives an auto point and a strike. A video will be provided showing what counts.
    Self-check

    Ask yourself every round

    • Have I dashed toward or around them in the last few seconds?
    • Am I just waiting for them to dash?
    • Have I only been counterdashing?
    • Am I in a corner, or pushing them into one?
    • Did I chain more than one ragdoll cancel?

    TermWorking definition
    M1Basic melee hit / attack string
